query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled annealing treatment that induces in-situ formation of ductile Fe–Co-rich precipitates along grain boundaries will improve the structural integrity of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 without impairing its caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy exhibiting a homogeneous phase but with inherent brittleness that results in cracking under mechanical stress.
generation.intervention: Apply a tailored annealing protocol at a temperature that is below the martensitic (or caloric transformation) transition yet high enough to promote precipitation, thereby generating a fine-scale, ductile Fe–Co-rich phase at grain boundaries and within grains.
generation.conditions: Under operating conditions that include applied magnetic or pressure fields and cyclic thermal conditions near ambient temperatures, with mechanical loading in compression similar to prior strength tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanometer-scale, ductile Fe–Co precipitates forming along grain boundaries and within the matrix, creating a crack‐arresting network.
generation.mechanism: The newly formed ductile precipitates are expected to enhance load transfer and arrest crack propagation by providing compliant interfaces at grain boundaries, thus improving compressive strength and overall durability while not interfering significantly with the primary phase transformation responsible for the caloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in compressive strength relative to the untreated alloy (potentially meeting or exceeding improvements achieved via epoxy or In composites) is predicted, with the caloric temperature change under applied field or pressure remaining comparable to that of the original alloy.
generation.baseline: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 in its as-cast or untreated homogeneous state exhibiting poor mechanical integrity and a high propensity for cracking.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only when the annealing temperature and duration are optimized so as not to trigger unwanted phase changes that could degrade the magneto- or baro-caloric effects. The outcome is bounded by operating conditions typical for field-, pressure-, and temperature-driven caloric cycles.
generation.uncertainty: The exact volume fraction, distribution, and interface quality of the Fe–Co precipitates achieved by the annealing treatment is uncertain, and its effect on the caloric efficiency needs experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples from the same starting material. Subject one batch to the proposed annealing treatment designed to precipitate ductile Fe–Co particles, while keeping the other batch untreated as a control. Both batches will then undergo identical tests under applied magnetic/pressure fields and thermal cycling.
measurements: Compressive strength using controlled mechanical tests
Caloric temperature change under field and pressure cycling
Microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM) to confirm the formation and distribution of Fe–Co precipitates
Thermal conductivity and related heat transport metrics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples fail to show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (i.e., compressive strength does not exceed that of the untreated alloy or does not reach benchmark levels observed in comparable composite systems) or if the caloric response is diminished relative to the control, the hypothesis will be falsified.
